## What HTML does HTML describes a document's content and structure. A browser reads that document and builds a page containing elements such as headings, paragraphs, links and lists. HTML is not the language that decides every colour or calculates an answer: CSS handles presentation and JavaScript adds programmable behaviour. Learning those jobs separately makes a page easier to understand and maintain. An element normally has an opening tag, some content and a closing tag. In `

Welcome

`, `p` identifies a paragraph and `Welcome` is its text. The closing slash belongs before the tag name. Nesting means placing one element inside another. Close an inner element before closing the element that contains it. ## Example 1: a complete document ```html My study page

My study page

I am learning to build accessible web pages.

``` Expected result: the preview displays a large heading followed by one paragraph. The title is document metadata, not another paragraph in the page. In a normal browser tab it supplies the tab title; an embedded practice preview does not need to replace the surrounding website's tab title. The doctype selects modern HTML document processing. `lang="en"` identifies the document's language. Character encoding supports text reliably, and viewport metadata lets the page use the device's available width. Content that readers interact with belongs inside `body`; document metadata belongs inside `head`. ## Example 2: headings explain a page's organisation ```html

Weekly study plan

Monday

Read the lesson and try its examples.

Tuesday

Review mistakes and complete the exercise.

``` Expected result: one main heading introduces two smaller section headings, each followed by a paragraph. Heading levels describe structure, not a desired font size. Use CSS later to change appearance without changing what a heading means. `main` identifies the principal content of this document. Try replacing the second paragraph's text. The rest of the structure should remain unchanged. This is a useful first debugging habit: change one thing, run again and compare the result with your prediction. ## Example 3: links connect meaningful content ```html

Revision checklist

Go to the practice section

Practice

Write a page with a heading and two paragraphs.

``` Expected result: a link labelled “Go to the practice section” targets the section with `id="practice"`. An attribute adds information to an opening tag. Here, `href` gives the link's destination and `id` names its target. This example needs no external network request. An anchor jump can be hard to notice when the entire short page already fits inside the preview. ## Mistakes, inspection and independent practice `

Read this

` is not the explicit closing syntax we intend; write `

Read this

`. Browsers recover from many HTML mistakes, so a visible result alone does not prove that the source is well structured. Check matching tags, nesting and attribute quotes as well as appearance. Never paste passwords, tokens or private information into practice examples. Build a study profile containing one main heading, a short introduction, two section headings and a link to the second section. Start from Example 1's document structure. Keep the source readable with indentation, but remember that indentation is for the person reading the source, not a substitute for elements. ```hint Put an id on the second section, then use the same name after # in the link's href. ``` ```solution One valid arrangement is a main element containing h1, an introductory p, a link with href="#goals", a first section, and a second section whose id is "goals". Both sections need descriptive h2 headings. There is no single required choice of personal text. ``` You are ready to continue when you can explain what belongs in `head` and `body`, write explicitly nested elements, and match a local link to its target without copying the examples line for line. ## Read the document, then test your prediction A browser does not infer a page section from the words in a link. It follows the address in href. A fragment beginning with # identifies a location in the current document. Compare that address against the target id character by character. This is different from naming a class for CSS. When a link appears to do nothing, a very short page might already show the target, or the target identifier might not exist. Check the structure before deciding that links are broken.

## JavaScript turns instructions into behaviour

JavaScript is a programming language used to calculate values, make decisions and respond to events. In a browser project, HTML supplies structure, CSS supplies presentation and JavaScript supplies programmable behaviour. The language can also run in other environments, so do not assume that every JavaScript program has a web page to manipulate.

This first lesson uses console mode. The practice runtime is isolated from the main website and prints output from `console.log`. It is not an unrestricted browser tab. Do not use external packages, network requests, `alert`, `prompt` or browser storage here. A later lesson introduces the separate Interactive DOM preview and its supported interfaces.

## Example 1: print an exact message

```javascript
console.log("Ready to practise");
console.log("Read, predict, run, compare");
```

Expected output:

```text
Ready to practise
Read, predict, run, compare
```

The quoted text is a string value. Its quote characters delimit the value; they do not appear in this output. Parentheses contain the value passed to `console.log`, and the dot accesses `log` on `console`. Each call writes its message to the output panel. Here, the semicolon marks the end of an instruction. JavaScript can insert some semicolons automatically, but explicit consistent punctuation is useful while learning.

## Example 2: compare numbers with numeric-looking text

```javascript
console.log(12 + 3);
console.log("12" + "3");
console.log(12 * 3);
```

Expected output:

```text
15
123
36
```

The first expression adds two numbers. The second joins two strings; quotation marks change the kind of value, even though the characters look numeric. The multiplication operator is an asterisk. Expressions are evaluated before their results are printed. Be precise about value types rather than relying on what a value looks like on screen. Later lessons cover conversion and the additional behaviours of operators in detail.

## Example 3: give values useful names

```javascript
const price = 150;
const quantity = 2;
const total = price * quantity;

console.log(total);
```

Expected output:

```text
300
```

`const` declares a binding with a name. The equals sign supplies its initial value; it is not an equality comparison. Read the instructions from top to bottom: `price` receives 150, `quantity` receives 2, and `total` receives the calculated product. Printing a name reads the value associated with it.

Use meaningful names such as `quantity`, not an unrelated label chosen only to shorten typing. JavaScript distinguishes uppercase and lowercase letters, so `Price` and `price` are different names. A `const` binding cannot be reassigned. Future lessons compare `const` with `let` and explain what this rule does and does not imply for objects.

## Errors provide clues

An unmatched quote or missing closing parenthesis can produce a syntax error before the intended output appears. Reading a name that has not been declared produces a different kind of error. Neither means that you should replace the whole program. Read the message, inspect the indicated area and compare the source against the intended instruction.

Try changing `quantity` to 4 in Example 3. Predict 600 before running it. Then change only the final call to `console.log(price)`. Predict 150: declaring `total` does not change the original price. This small experiment separates calculating a new value from changing an existing one.

## Independent exercise

Write a program that declares a ticket price and a ticket count, calculates a total and prints it. Add a separate printed heading describing the calculation. Use only numbers, strings, `const`, multiplication and `console.log`; do not introduce input boxes or DOM operations yet.

```hint
Start with two constant declarations. Give the product its own name before printing it, so each step has a clear purpose.
```

```solution
For example, const ticketPrice = 200; const ticketCount = 3; const ticketTotal = ticketPrice * ticketCount; followed by console.log("Ticket total"); and console.log(ticketTotal); prints a heading and then 600. Different sensible names and values are valid.
```

## Trace a value before trusting its appearance

A console displays characters, but the program operates on values with types. The same digits can be a number in one expression and a string in another. Read the quotation marks in the source before predicting what + will do. Named results are also values, not live spreadsheet formulas. The program calculates the expression at the moment that instruction executes. Reading an input binding to calculate a new total does not change that input binding. Keep those ideas separate when debugging an unexpected result.

## PHP and the environment running it

PHP is a programming language commonly used on web servers. In a normal web application, a server runs the PHP program and sends its output to a browser. The browser does not run the server's PHP source merely because someone included it in an HTML file.

Our practice editor uses a PHP interpreter compiled to WebAssembly, running in your browser. This lets you practise language features without renting a server. It does not create a public PHP backend, connect to a production database or reproduce every web-server feature. Later lessons distinguish portable language examples from examples that require a separate server environment. Never put production credentials into a practice program.

## Example 1: produce plain text

```php
<?php
echo "Welcome to PHP\n";
echo "Run one example at a time.\n";
```

Expected output:

```text
Welcome to PHP
Run one example at a time.
```

`<?php` starts PHP code. `echo` writes output, and each semicolon ends a statement. The double-quoted `\n` escape produces a newline in this text output. In a file containing only PHP, leaving out the closing PHP tag is an established way to avoid accidentally emitting trailing material outside the program.

The output panel here displays text. In a web application, the context consuming output matters: an HTML response interprets markup and normally collapses ordinary whitespace. A newline in text output is not a universal substitute for an HTML element.

## Example 2: calculate before printing

```php
<?php
echo 8 + 4;
echo "\n";
echo 8 * 4;
echo "\n";
```

Expected output:

```text
12
32
```

Arithmetic expressions produce values before `echo` writes them. The plus sign performs addition here, and the asterisk performs multiplication. The numbers are not quoted strings. Later lessons explain types, numeric conversion and operator precedence; for now, use deliberate simple expressions so the result is unambiguous.

Predict the result after changing only the first expression to `(8 + 4) * 2`. Parentheses make that grouping explicit. It should print 24 on the first output line while the second calculation remains unchanged.

## Example 3: named values make calculations readable

```php
<?php
$price = 120;
$quantity = 3;
$total = $price * $quantity;

echo "Total: ";
echo $total;
echo "\n";
```

Expected output:

```text
Total: 360
```

PHP variable names begin with `$`. The assignment operator associates a value with the variable. Read this example as a sequence: establish a price, establish a quantity, calculate their product, then write the label and result. Variables make it possible to change an input value without hunting for unrelated repeated numbers.

Variable names are case-sensitive. `$price` and `$Price` do not identify the same variable. Use descriptive consistent names, and initialise each variable before reading it. A misspelled name can produce a diagnostic even when a similar-looking name was assigned earlier.

## Debugging and boundaries

Start by checking the opening tag, matching quotes, variable spelling and semicolons. A parser error near a later line can originate from an earlier missing quote or semicolon. Change one fault at a time and run the program again. Do not hide diagnostic messages to make a broken example appear successful.

This lesson needs no file reads, database connection or network request. Keeping the first programs self-contained makes their behaviour reproducible in the browser interpreter and on a suitably configured PHP installation.

## Independent exercise

Declare a notebook price and a notebook quantity. Calculate a total and print a readable label followed by the total and a newline. Choose your own sensible positive values. Explain which lines set input values and which line calculates the result.

```hint
Every reference to a PHP variable needs its dollar sign. Keep the arithmetic separate from the output statements so you can inspect each step.
```

```solution
With $notebookPrice = 75; and $notebookQuantity = 4;, assigning their product to $notebookTotal and echoing that value produces 300. Add an explicit text label and a newline using separate echo statements.
```

## Connect a PHP statement to its output

The interpreter runs the PHP instructions, and echo writes the output they produce. The browser practice runtime is an interpreter, not a public web server. That distinction matters when reading examples elsewhere: a form, session or database example can depend on server configuration that this isolated exercise does not supply. Here the inputs are explicit variables, so you can reproduce each calculation without hidden environment state. Follow the dollar signs, statement boundaries and output calls rather than guessing from the final text.

## A program is a sequence of instructions

Python lets you express calculations and other operations as readable instructions. The interpreter reads and executes a program according to the language's rules. Small programs are useful because you can predict each instruction's effect and compare that prediction with the actual result.

The practice editor runs Python through Pyodide inside an isolated browser runtime. These examples need only the bundled interpreter. They do not need package installation, external network access or persistent files. Later lessons will explain the standard library and distinguish portable language exercises from programs needing additional services.

## Example 1: print strings

```python
print("Learning Python")
print("Predict before you run")
```

Expected output:

```text
Learning Python
Predict before you run
```

The quoted text is a string. `print` receives the value inside its parentheses and writes it to the output panel. In this example each call ends its output with a newline, so the messages occupy separate lines. The quotes identify the string in source code but are not part of the printed message.

You can use either matching single quotes or matching double quotes for these simple strings. Start and finish a string deliberately; an unmatched quote causes a syntax error. Copying a sentence from a word processor can introduce typographic quotation marks that are not the ordinary source-code delimiters shown here.

## Example 2: numbers and strings are different values

```python
print(10 + 5)
print("10" + "5")
print(10 * 5)
```

Expected output:

```text
15
105
50
```

The first line adds numbers. The second joins strings; adding quote marks changes the kind of value the program is working with. The third line multiplies numbers using `*`. Python evaluates the expression before passing its result to `print`.

Do not guess a value's type merely from the characters displayed in output. A printed string containing digits can look like a printed number. Later lessons use explicit type inspection and conversion to make that distinction visible. For now, read the source and identify which values have string delimiters.

## Example 3: calculate with named values

```python
price = 90
quantity = 4
total = price * quantity

print(total)
```

Expected output:

```text
360
```

The equals sign is assignment: it binds the name on the left to the value calculated on the right. It does not ask whether two things are equal. The first two lines establish inputs, the third calculates a result, and the final line displays that result.

Names are case-sensitive. `quantity` and `Quantity` are different names. Choose clear names and use them consistently. Python does not require a dollar sign or a `const` keyword for these assignments. We will investigate names, changing values and object behaviour in more depth in subsequent lessons.

## Reason about execution order

If you change `quantity` to 5 before the `total` assignment, the product becomes 450. If you add `quantity = 5` after the `total` assignment, printing the existing `total` still gives 360: the earlier calculation is not a spreadsheet formula that automatically recalculates whenever another name changes.

To calculate using the new quantity, execute the multiplication assignment again. Predict this behaviour, edit one example and verify it. Understanding execution order is more valuable than memorising the sample numbers.

## Mistakes and independent practice

Check matching parentheses and quotes when a syntax error occurs. Check spelling and execution order when a name is not defined. Do not indent every line randomly: indentation has a structural role in Python, which we will study with conditional statements and loops. The top-level statements in this lesson start at the left margin.

Write a program that names a number of study days and a number of minutes per day, calculates total minutes and prints both a label and the result. Use only assignments, multiplication, strings and `print`.

```hint
Calculate total_minutes = study_days * minutes_per_day after assigning both input names.
```

```solution
For study_days = 5 and minutes_per_day = 30, the multiplication gives 150. A separate print("Planned study minutes") call can label the number printed by print(total_minutes).
```

## A named result is not an automatically updating formula

Execution order is one of the most useful mental models for a beginner. Python evaluates an assignment when it reaches that instruction. A total calculated earlier does not automatically update just because a different input name receives a new value afterwards. That behaviour is different from a spreadsheet cell that contains a continuing formula. You must execute the calculation again when you need a new result. Trace this distinction carefully before introducing loops or functions, because those later tools still rely on the same execution model.

## Understand the idea

A type describes the kind of value an operation receives, not how its output happens to look. The integer 12 and the string "12" print similar characters, but adding two integers calculates a sum while adding two strings joins text. Start by identifying literal syntax, then inspect type(value) when you need evidence. Do not fix every error by converting everything to a string: decide whether the next operation needs text or a number.

Conversion is an explicit request to construct a value of another type. int("12") parses suitable integer text; str(12) constructs text; float("2.5") parses a decimal representation. Conversion can fail. int("twelve") raises ValueError because those characters are not integer syntax. int(2.9) truncates towards zero; it does not round to the nearest integer. Keep those operations distinct.

For a study-duration calculation, a numeric total should stay numeric until it is formatted for display. Store converted inputs under clear names rather than repeatedly converting the same text inside a long expression. This makes the point where validation belongs easier to find. Floating-point values also have finite precision, so printed decimal examples are not a promise of exact decimal arithmetic for money.

## Example 1: Inspect the type

```python
value = "12"
print(type(value).__name__)
print(type(12).__name__)
```

Expected output:

```text
str
int
```

The first literal has quotation marks and produces a string. The second is an integer. __name__ gives the type name without the class wrapper that type itself displays. The printed digits alone would not reveal this distinction.

## Example 2: Calculate after parsing

```python
days_text = "5"
days = int(days_text)
print(days * 30)
print(days_text * 2)
```

Expected output:

```text
150
55
```

Multiplying the parsed integer performs arithmetic. Multiplying the original string by an integer repeats the text. The original variable is not changed by constructing another value with int.

## Example 3: Format only at the boundary

```python
minutes = 150
message = "Minutes: " + str(minutes)
print(message)
print(int(2.9))
```

Expected output:

```text
Minutes: 150
2
```

The total becomes text only for concatenation. The last line demonstrates truncation, which differs from rounding. Use the operation whose documented behaviour matches the problem.

## Understand the idea

A string is an immutable sequence of Unicode code points. Indexing chooses one position, beginning at zero. Negative indices count back from the end, so -1 selects the last character of a nonempty string. Immutability means assigning text[0] = "X" does not edit a character in place. Construct a new string when you want changed text.

A slice describes a range using start:stop, where stop is excluded. Leaving start empty begins at the start; leaving stop empty continues to the end. Slicing is forgiving when a boundary extends beyond the string, but indexing a missing position raises IndexError. These are different operations, not inconsistent handling of the same request.

Methods such as strip and lower return new strings. Assign their result when you need to keep it. strip removes leading and trailing whitespace, not every space inside a sentence. Work through a short concrete example before combining several methods. A visible character can contain multiple Unicode code points, so advanced text editing needs more care than assuming every index corresponds to one user-perceived character.

## Example 1: Read positions

```python
word = "Python"
print(word[0])
print(word[-1])
print(len(word))
```

Expected output:

```text
P
n
6
```

P occupies index zero and n is the last character. len reports the sequence length. These ASCII characters each occupy one code point, making the index model easy to inspect.

## Example 2: Take a slice

```python
word = "Python"
print(word[1:4])
print(word[:2])
print(word[4:])
```

Expected output:

```text
yth
Py
on
```

The first slice includes indices one, two and three, but not four. The omitted bounds in the next two slices mean start of string and end of string respectively. The original word remains unchanged.

## Example 3: Keep a method result

```python
label = "  Study Time  "
clean = label.strip().lower()
print(clean)
print(label.startswith("  "))
```

Expected output:

```text
study time
True
```

The cleaned value is a new string. The original label still starts with spaces. lower changes letter case; strip removes only the surrounding whitespace in this example.

## Check the reasoning

A slice excludes its stop position and returns a new string.

## Understand the idea

An operator describes an operation on operands. Arithmetic operators calculate values; comparison operators produce booleans. Assignment with = binds a name, while == compares values. Read those symbols deliberately rather than treating every equals sign as a question. Python uses ** for exponentiation; ^ is a bitwise operator, not a power symbol.

For integer operands, // computes floor division and % computes the corresponding remainder. Floor division moves towards negative infinity, which matters for negative numbers. The examples begin with positive counts so you can check the quotient and remainder against a concrete grouping problem. Parentheses make grouping explicit when an expression contains several operations.

Boolean operators and, or and not combine truth tests. and and or short-circuit and actually return an operand, so avoid assuming every use constructs a bool. When you want a boolean condition, use clear comparison expressions on each side. Write a range check as 0 <= score <= 100 rather than accidentally checking only one boundary. Prefer a readable condition over a compressed expression that nobody can confidently trace.

## Example 1: Group arithmetic explicitly

```python
print(2 + 3 * 4)
print((2 + 3) * 4)
print(2 ** 3)
```

Expected output:

```text
14
20
8
```

Multiplication happens before addition in the first expression. Parentheses change the grouping in the second. The third expression calculates a power, using two asterisks.

## Example 2: Count complete groups

```python
minutes = 95
print(minutes // 30)
print(minutes % 30)
```

Expected output:

```text
3
5
```

Ninety-five minutes contains three complete thirty-minute blocks and five remaining minutes. This positive example provides a concrete interpretation of quotient and remainder.

## Example 3: Compare a score

```python
score = 80
print(score >= 80)
print(0 <= score <= 100)
print(score == 100)
```

Expected output:

```text
True
True
False
```

The passing boundary includes 80. The chained comparison checks both limits. Comparing with 100 is a separate question and does not modify score.

## Check the reasoning

Assignment binds a name; comparison evaluates a relationship between values.

## Understand the idea

A conditional selects which suite of instructions runs. An if statement evaluates its condition; elif provides another test when earlier tests did not match; else handles the remaining case. In one if/elif/else chain, only the first matching branch runs. Separate if statements are separate decisions and may all run. Choose the structure that expresses the problem.

A colon introduces each branch suite, and consistent indentation groups its statements. Four spaces per level is the conventional style used here. Indentation is syntax, not decoration. A line dedented back to the outer level runs after the decision rather than belonging to the last branch. Avoid mixing tabs and spaces.

Think about boundaries before writing a condition. If 80 passes, test 79, 80 and 81. If grades are ordered from strongest to weakest, place the strongest threshold first; otherwise a high score may satisfy an earlier weaker condition. Validation is a separate concern: an impossible score such as 150 should not silently receive the highest valid grade. These small test cases expose logic defects that a single happy-path example can hide.

## Example 1: Include the passing boundary

```python
score = 80
if score >= 80:
    print("Pass")
else:
    print("Retry")
print("Test finished")
```

Expected output:

```text
Pass
Test finished
```

The first branch includes the boundary value. The final print is outside both branches, so it runs after the decision regardless of the selected branch.

## Example 2: Order thresholds

```python
score = 92
if score >= 90:
    print("Excellent")
elif score >= 80:
    print("Passed")
else:
    print("Keep practising")
```

Expected output:

```text
Excellent
```

A score of 92 also exceeds 80, but the first branch already matched. The interpreter does not execute the elif branch in the same chain.

## Example 3: Reject an invalid range

```python
score = 105
if not 0 <= score <= 100:
    print("Invalid score")
elif score >= 80:
    print("Pass")
else:
    print("Retry")
```

Expected output:

```text
Invalid score
```

Range validation happens before grading. A large numeric value is not automatically a valid score. This is an example of checking domain constraints, not just data types.

## Check the reasoning

Only the first matching branch of one if/elif/else chain executes.

## Understand the idea

A loop repeats instructions according to a defined iteration rule. A for loop visits items from an iterable; range supplies a sequence of integers without building a list of all of them. range(stop) begins at zero and excludes stop. range(start, stop) uses an explicit beginning and still excludes the end. This boundary convention is consistent with slicing.

A while loop repeats while its condition is true. Something inside or outside the loop must eventually change that condition if the program is meant to finish. Update the controlling state deliberately and trace the smallest input before increasing the workload. The browser practice runtime stops unresponsive code, but a timeout is a safety net, not correct loop design.

An accumulator stores a running result. Initialise it before the loop, then update it on each iteration. Resetting it inside the loop discards earlier work. break exits the nearest loop; continue skips to its next iteration. Use either only when it clarifies the logic. When a loop is wrong, write down the variable values after each iteration instead of changing its start and stop numbers at random.

## Example 1: Inspect range boundaries

```python
for day in range(1, 4):
    print(day)
```

Expected output:

```text
1
2
3
```

The sequence begins at one and stops before four. Three instructions print on three iterations. A for loop gives day a new item value each time.

## Example 2: Build a running total

```python
total = 0
for minutes in range(10, 31, 10):
    total += minutes
print(total)
```

Expected output:

```text
60
```

The step is ten, so the loop visits ten, twenty and thirty. The single total initialised before the loop accumulates all three values. The final print is outside the loop.

## Example 3: Make a while loop terminate

```python
remaining = 3
while remaining > 0:
    print(remaining)
    remaining -= 1
print("Done")
```

Expected output:

```text
3
2
1
Done
```

Each iteration decreases the controlling value. Once it reaches zero the condition is false, and execution moves to the final print. Omitting the update would make this example unbounded.

## Check the reasoning

range excludes its stop value, and a running total must be initialised before iteration.

## Understand the idea

A list stores an ordered collection of references to values. Indexing and slicing use the same zero-based, stop-excluded conventions you studied for strings. Unlike strings, lists are mutable: you can replace an element, append another one or remove an item. Mutation changes the existing list rather than necessarily constructing a new list.

Names can refer to the same mutable object. Assigning alias = scores does not copy every element into an independent collection. A mutation through alias is visible through scores because both names refer to the same list. scores.copy() creates a shallow copy of the outer list. Nested mutable objects can still be shared, so do not describe shallow copying as complete recursive independence.

Methods have different return contracts. append changes the list and returns None; it does not return the updated list. Write scores.append(90), then inspect scores. Assigning scores = scores.append(90) loses the original list binding by replacing it with None. When processing a collection, avoid removing items from the same list while iterating over it unless you have carefully defined the algorithm. A separate result list is usually easier for a beginner to reason about.

## Example 1: Append and replace

```python
scores = [70, 80]
scores.append(90)
scores[0] = 75
print(scores)
```

Expected output:

```text
[75, 80, 90]
```

append adds an element at the end. The indexed assignment changes the first existing element. The list keeps its order and now has three elements.

## Example 2: Inspect aliasing

```python
scores = [70, 80]
alias = scores
alias.append(90)
print(scores)
print(alias is scores)
```

Expected output:

```text
[70, 80, 90]
True
```

Both names refer to the same object. The is comparison checks identity here; it does not merely compare the text representation of the lists.

## Example 3: Copy the outer list

```python
scores = [70, 80]
copy = scores.copy()
copy.append(90)
print(scores)
print(copy)
```

Expected output:

```text
[70, 80]
[70, 80, 90]
```

Appending to the separate outer list does not append to the original. These lists contain only integers, so the nested-sharing limitation does not complicate this particular example.

## Check the reasoning

Assignment shares the same list reference; a shallow copy creates a separate outer list.

## Understand the idea

A tuple is an ordered sequence whose element references cannot be replaced after construction. It is useful for a small record whose positions have a stable meaning, such as a label and a duration returned together. A tuple can still contain a mutable object; immutability of the outer tuple does not freeze everything nested inside it.

The comma is what forms a tuple in a single-value expression. (5) is the integer five in grouping parentheses; (5,) is a one-element tuple. Parentheses make tuple syntax readable, especially inside other expressions. Empty parentheses form the empty tuple.

Unpacking binds several names from an iterable in one assignment. The number of unstarred targets must match the number of values. A starred target can collect remaining values into a list. Choose descriptive target names because positional data otherwise becomes hard to interpret. Unpacking is not limited to tuples, but a tuple provides a clear first example. If a record develops many fields or unclear positions, a named structure may be more appropriate.

## Example 1: Unpack a small record

```python
session = ("Python", 30)
subject, minutes = session
print(subject)
print(minutes)
```

Expected output:

```text
Python
30
```

The first item binds to subject and the second to minutes. Unpacking does not remove items from the original tuple or change its length.

## Example 2: Notice the comma

```python
single = (5,)
grouped = (5)
print(type(single).__name__)
print(type(grouped).__name__)
```

Expected output:

```text
tuple
int
```

The trailing comma creates a one-item tuple. Parentheses alone can group an ordinary expression and do not necessarily create a tuple.

## Example 3: Collect remaining items

```python
first, *remaining = (10, 20, 30)
print(first)
print(remaining)
```

Expected output:

```text
10
[20, 30]
```

The first target receives one item. The starred target receives a list containing the remaining items, even though the source collection is a tuple.

## Check the reasoning

Tuple unpacking binds names to sequence items; a single-item tuple needs a comma.

## Understand the idea

A dictionary associates keys with values. Use it when a descriptive lookup key expresses the relationship better than a numeric position. A subject-to-duration mapping lets you request the minutes for Python directly without remembering which list index represents Python. Keys must be hashable, and each key occurs at most once in the mapping. Assigning an existing key replaces its associated value.

Index-style lookup with mapping[key] raises KeyError if the key is missing. get(key, default) provides an explicit fallback. Do not use a fallback that hides a genuine data defect: zero minutes may be a meaningful result rather than a useful substitute for missing configuration. Decide whether absence is acceptable in this part of the program.

Dictionary iteration preserves insertion order in modern Python. Looping over a dictionary yields keys; items() gives key-value pairs for unpacking. Membership with in checks keys, not all stored values. Keep these contracts distinct. When displaying results, use a clear order if the domain requires sorting rather than depending accidentally on the order in which input arrived.

## Example 1: Read and update a key

```python
minutes = {"Python": 30, "HTML": 20}
minutes["Python"] = 40
print(minutes["Python"])
print(len(minutes))
```

Expected output:

```text
40
2
```

The assignment updates an existing key rather than adding a third entry. A dictionary contains one associated value for each distinct key.

## Example 2: Handle a missing key

```python
minutes = {"Python": 30}
print(minutes.get("CSS", 0))
print("Python" in minutes)
print(30 in minutes)
```

Expected output:

```text
0
True
False
```

get returns the chosen default for the missing CSS key. Membership checks keys, so the stored numeric value 30 is not itself a matching key.

## Example 3: Visit key-value pairs

```python
minutes = {"Python": 30, "HTML": 20}
for subject, duration in minutes.items():
    print(subject, duration)
```

Expected output:

```text
Python 30
HTML 20
```

items provides pairs that the loop unpacks. The output follows the insertion order in this example. The dictionary is not sorted alphabetically automatically.

## Check the reasoning

Dictionary membership checks keys, and get can supply an explicit missing-key fallback.

## Understand the idea

A set represents distinct hashable values with membership as a central operation. It is useful for questions such as which subjects appear in both a requested and an available collection. It does not provide a positional sequence interface and does not promise an iteration order suitable for a stable display.

Construct an empty set with set(). Empty braces create an empty dictionary instead. Repeated values collapse into a single set member. That makes a set useful for deduplication when you do not need the original ordering or duplicate count. If either matters, keep the original sequence and choose an algorithm that preserves the information you need.

Union combines members from either set; intersection keeps common members; difference keeps members from the left that are absent on the right. Those operations return new sets. For reproducible printed examples, sort the result before displaying it. remove raises KeyError for an absent member; discard tolerates its absence. Choosing the latter can be appropriate when absence is expected, but it should not silently hide a broken invariant.

## Example 1: Remove duplicates intentionally

```python
subjects = {"Python", "HTML", "Python"}
print(len(subjects))
print("Python" in subjects)
```

Expected output:

```text
2
True
```

The repeated Python value does not create another member. The membership test asks whether that value belongs to the set, not where it appears.

## Example 2: Compare two collections

```python
requested = {"Python", "CSS"}
available = {"Python", "HTML"}
print(sorted(requested & available))
print(sorted(requested - available))
```

Expected output:

```text
['Python']
['CSS']
```

Intersection identifies the available requested subject. Difference identifies what is requested but unavailable. Sorting makes the display deterministic without claiming that the set itself is ordered.

## Example 3: Create and update an empty set

```python
completed = set()
completed.add("HTML")
completed.add("HTML")
completed.discard("CSS")
print(sorted(completed))
```

Expected output:

```text
['HTML']
```

Adding the same member again changes nothing. discard permits the absent CSS member. The empty collection is explicitly a set, not an empty dictionary.

## Check the reasoning

A set stores distinct members, not a promised display order or indexed sequence.

## Understand the idea

A function gives a reusable operation a name. Its definition describes parameters and a body; calling it supplies arguments and executes that body. Merely defining a function does not run its calculation. Keep the purpose small enough that you can explain the input and output contract in a sentence.

return sends a value back to the caller and exits the current function call. print writes a display side effect; it is not a replacement for returning a value that another calculation needs. A function without an explicit returned value returns None. This distinction matters when you want to combine operations instead of displaying everything immediately.

Local names created during a call are separate from the caller names that supplied values. Avoid relying on unrelated global variables when an argument would make the dependency explicit. Functions are easier to test when the same explicit input produces the same result without changing outside state. Later lessons introduce more parameter rules and scope behaviour, but a clear calculation and return is the best starting point.

## Example 1: Return a calculated result

```python
def study_total(days, minutes):
    return days * minutes

result = study_total(5, 30)
print(result)
```

Expected output:

```text
150
```

The function receives two arguments, computes their product and returns it. The caller chooses to print the returned result. No output occurs merely from defining study_total.

## Example 2: Recognise an implicit None

```python
def show_message():
    print("Ready")

result = show_message()
print(result)
```

Expected output:

```text
Ready
None
```

The function displays Ready but has no explicit return expression. The caller therefore receives None, which the final print makes visible.

## Example 3: Compose returned values

```python
def double(value):
    return value * 2

print(double(10) + double(5))
```

Expected output:

```text
30
```

Each call returns a number. The addition combines those numbers before the outer print displays the total. This would not work the same way if double only printed its result.

## Check the reasoning

return supplies a value to the caller; print only displays a value.

If the result differs, find the first instruction where your prediction stops matching the program state. Keep that small case as a regression check when you fix the cause.

## Understand the idea

Parameters name the inputs a function accepts. Positional arguments are matched by position, while keyword arguments identify their parameter names explicitly. A default provides a value when the caller omits that argument. Choose defaults that make sense for the operation rather than using them to hide a required decision.

Default expressions are evaluated when the function definition executes, not freshly on every call. A mutable default such as items=[] can therefore be shared across calls. Use None as a sentinel and construct a new list inside the function when each omitted argument should mean a fresh collection. Passing an existing list intentionally still permits the function to mutate that list, so document that contract.

Assignments inside a function normally create local bindings. Reading an outer value is different from assigning an outer binding. Prefer returning a new value and assigning it in the caller over reaching for global state. This keeps the source of a change visible and makes the function easier to reuse. A function parameter is a local name bound to the supplied object, not an automatic deep copy of that object.

## Example 1: Use a default intentionally

```python
def total(days, minutes=30):
    return days * minutes

print(total(5))
print(total(minutes=20, days=3))
```

Expected output:

```text
150
60
```

The omitted minutes argument receives its default on the first call. Explicit keywords make the second call readable without depending on argument order.

## Example 2: Build a fresh optional list

```python
def record(value, items=None):
    if items is None:
        items = []
    items.append(value)
    return items

print(record("HTML"))
print(record("Python"))
```

Expected output:

```text
['HTML']
['Python']
```

Each omitted items argument causes a new list to be constructed inside that call. The second result does not accidentally contain the first call’s subject.

## Example 3: Separate local and caller bindings

```python
minutes = 30

def adjust(value):
    minutes = value + 5
    return minutes

print(adjust(10))
print(minutes)
```

Expected output:

```text
15
30
```

The assignment in adjust creates a local name. Returning its value does not overwrite the caller’s minutes binding. The caller can explicitly store the result if that is desired.

## Check the reasoning

Use a fresh collection inside the call instead of a mutable default shared between calls.

## Understand the idea

A comprehension constructs a collection from an iterable using an expression and optional filtering conditions. Read a simple list comprehension as: evaluate the leading expression for each item that passes the filter. It is a compact collection-building tool, not a requirement to replace every loop.

The expression determines what enters the result; the filter determines whether an input participates. These roles are separate. An if after the iterable filters items, while a conditional expression before for chooses between output values. Start with a normal loop if the distinction is not yet clear. Name the source collection and result so the transformation can be explained.

List, set and dictionary comprehensions build different collection types. A dictionary comprehension creates key-value associations, and duplicate keys overwrite earlier values just as in other dictionary construction. Avoid side effects inside a comprehension. If the code is mainly printing, updating unrelated state or handling several branches, an explicit loop usually communicates the intent better. Compact syntax is useful only when the reader can still reason about the operation.

## Example 1: Transform each input

```python
minutes = [10, 20, 30]
doubled = [value * 2 for value in minutes]
print(doubled)
print(minutes)
```

Expected output:

```text
[20, 40, 60]
[10, 20, 30]
```

The expression multiplies each number before it enters the new list. The original list is not changed by this construction.

## Example 2: Filter before collecting

```python
scores = [65, 80, 92]
passed = [score for score in scores if score >= 80]
print(passed)
```

Expected output:

```text
[80, 92]
```

Only values satisfying the inclusive passing condition enter the result. The leading expression is score, so the included numeric values are retained without another transformation.

## Example 3: Build named associations

```python
subjects = ["HTML", "Python"]
lengths = {subject: len(subject) for subject in subjects}
print(lengths["HTML"])
print(lengths["Python"])
```

Expected output:

```text
4
6
```

The comprehension produces a dictionary, not a list. Each subject becomes a key associated with its character count, and the prints perform explicit key lookups.

## Check the reasoning

The comprehension expression transforms each included item; its trailing condition filters inputs.

## Understand the idea

An exception signals that an operation could not complete normally. It interrupts the current path until an appropriate handler is found. A syntax error in your program and a ValueError while parsing external text are different problems; do not treat every failure as something to ignore and continue past.

A try suite contains the operation that may fail. An except clause handles a specified exception class. Keep the protected operation small enough that the handler’s meaning stays clear. Catching Exception around the whole program can conceal unrelated bugs, such as a misspelled name in the recovery logic. Catch the failures that the program can actually recover from.

The else suite runs if the try suite completes without an exception. finally runs as execution leaves the try statement, whether the operation succeeded or failed. It is useful for cleanup, but a context manager is often clearer for resource management. A recovery value must make sense in the domain: returning zero for invalid exam data can silently convert a bad record into an apparently valid score. Prefer an explicit invalid result when that distinction matters.

## Example 1: Handle invalid integer text

```python
text = "twelve"
try:
    value = int(text)
except ValueError:
    print("Enter integer digits")
```

Expected output:

```text
Enter integer digits
```

int cannot parse this word as an integer, so ValueError selects the handler. The program displays an actionable message instead of pretending conversion succeeded.

## Example 2: Separate success and cleanup

```python
try:
    value = int("12")
except ValueError:
    print("Invalid")
else:
    print(value * 2)
finally:
    print("Checked")
```

Expected output:

```text
24
Checked
```

Conversion succeeds, so else runs. finally then runs on exit from the statement. No Invalid message is printed because the except branch was not selected.

## Example 3: Raise a domain error

```python
def checked_minutes(value):
    if value < 0:
        raise ValueError("Minutes cannot be negative")
    return value

try:
    checked_minutes(-5)
except ValueError as error:
    print(str(error))
```

Expected output:

```text
Minutes cannot be negative
```

The value is numeric but invalid for the application’s domain. Raising an explicit error distinguishes this situation from a successful duration calculation.

## Check the reasoning

Catch a specific expected failure and make recovery explicit rather than hiding unrelated errors.

A matching screenshot or output is one check, not proof that a program is correct for all inputs. Change one input, predict the new result and run again. If the result differs, find the first instruction where your prediction stops matching the program state. Keep that small case as a regression check when you fix the cause.

## Understand the idea

A module provides a namespace that groups related definitions. Importing a module binds a name through which you can access its members. Using math.isqrt makes both the operation and its source visible; importing one selected name can be convenient when that name remains unambiguous in the surrounding code.

The standard library ships with Python, but availability still depends on the execution environment. Browser practice is not an unrestricted operating-system shell. Do not assume that every standard-library feature can access files, spawn processes or contact networks here. Third-party packages are not automatically available just because an example on the internet imports them.

Avoid wildcard imports in introductory application code because they hide where names came from and can overwrite existing bindings. Do not name your own source file math.py or json.py when you intend to import the standard-library module of that name: local naming conflicts can produce confusing behaviour. Imports can execute module-level code, so shared modules should avoid unexpected work at import time. A main guard lets a module distinguish direct execution from being imported by another program.

## Example 1: Use a module namespace

```python
import math
print(math.isqrt(81))
print(math.ceil(2.2))
```

Expected output:

```text
9
3
```

isqrt gives the integer square root, and ceil rounds upward to an integer. Prefixing both names with math makes their origin explicit.

## Example 2: Import one selected name

```python
from math import gcd
print(gcd(18, 24))
```

Expected output:

```text
6
```

gcd becomes a name in the current namespace. This is not the same spelling as importing math and then calling math.gcd, although both access the same standard-library operation.

## Example 3: Inspect a familiar namespace

```python
import string
print(string.ascii_lowercase[:3])
print(string.digits)
```

Expected output:

```text
abc
0123456789
```

The module also exposes useful constant values, not only functions. The slice uses the same stop-excluded rule already studied for strings.

## Check the reasoning

Importing a module provides a namespace; it does not make every external package or system capability available.

A matching screenshot or output is one check, not proof that a program is correct for all inputs. Change one input, predict the new result and run again. ## Understand the idea

The standard library contains focused tools that prevent unnecessary reinvention. Choose a tool by its input and output contract rather than importing a large collection of names and guessing which one might work. statistics.mean computes an arithmetic mean; collections.Counter counts occurrences; itertools can build controlled iteration patterns. Each solves a different problem.

A count is not the same statistic as an average. If duplicate subjects are meaningful events, converting to a set before counting destroys useful frequency information. Likewise, an average can hide variation: two students with very different scores may have the same mean as a consistent student. Report a measure only when it answers the question you are asking.

Inspect edge cases before relying on an operation. An empty data collection may require an explicit decision instead of a default that looks like a valid measurement. Iterators can also be consumed; converting a tiny iterator to a list is useful for inspection, but building enormous collections defeats their purpose. These examples are deliberately bounded and deterministic, requiring no external packages or network services.

```python
from statistics import mean
minutes = [20, 30, 40]
print(mean(minutes))
```

Expected output:

```text
30
```

The sum of the three durations is ninety and the item count is three. mean computes their arithmetic average. This does not imply that each session lasted thirty minutes.

## Example 2: Count repeated values

```python
from collections import Counter
counts = Counter(["Python", "HTML", "Python"])
print(counts["Python"])
print(counts["CSS"])
```

Expected output:

```text

0
```

Counter retains frequency rather than discarding repeats. Its missing-member count is zero, a deliberate contract that differs from ordinary dictionary bracket lookup.

## Example 3: Pair consecutive values

```python
from itertools import pairwise
for previous, current in pairwise([10, 15, 25]):
    print(current - previous)
```

Expected output:

```text
5
10
```

## Understand the idea

JSON is a text data format, not executable Python source. json.loads parses JSON text into Python values; json.dumps serialises compatible values into JSON text. JSON true, false and null map to Python True, False and None. Object keys are text, and JSON does not preserve arbitrary Python object types.

Parsing is not complete validation. A syntactically valid JSON document can still have missing fields, unexpected types or unreasonable sizes. Check the shape and domain constraints before treating data as a trusted record. Never use eval to parse text received from a user or a remote system. The JSON parser is built for this job and does not need to execute source code.

File access also has an environment boundary. The practice interpreter uses an isolated virtual filesystem and does not promise persistence after a session or reload. To demonstrate the file interface without changing any real files, these examples use io.StringIO. Its with statement shows a context-managed text stream that is closed afterward. A production program using real paths would additionally need explicit encoding, path boundaries, size limits and an appropriate storage lifecycle.

## Example 1: Read JSON data

```python
import json
record = json.loads('{"subject":"Python","minutes":30,"done":true}')
print(record["subject"])
print(record["done"])
```

Expected output:

```text
Python
True
```

The JSON boolean becomes a Python bool. The parsed dictionary can be queried with normal key access, but a real application should still verify required keys and value types.

## Example 2: Serialise predictably

```python
import json
record = {"minutes": 30, "done": False}
print(json.dumps(record, sort_keys=True))
```

Expected output:

```text
{"done": false, "minutes": 30}
```

dumps creates a JSON string. Sorting keys makes this example’s output stable; it does not change the dictionary’s meaning or add validation.

## Example 3: Read a bounded text stream

```python
from io import StringIO
with StringIO("Python\nHTML\n") as stream:
    first = stream.readline().strip()
    second = stream.readline().strip()
    print(first)
    print(second)
print(stream.closed)
```

Expected output:

```text
Python
HTML
True
```

The stream contains fixed in-memory text, not a persistent external file. readline reads one line at a time, and leaving the context closes the stream.

## Check the reasoning

JSON parsing constructs data, not executable source, and parsed records still need validation.

A matching screenshot or output is one check, not proof that a program is correct for all inputs. Change one input, predict the new result and run again. ## Understand the idea

A class defines a type whose instances can hold related state and behaviour. Use it when the relationship between the data and operations becomes clearer, not merely because classes look more advanced. A small dictionary and a function can be the better design for a simple one-off calculation.

__init__ initialises an instance after it is created. The conventional first parameter self refers to the instance receiving the method call. Assigning self.name creates or updates an attribute on that instance. By contrast, a mutable attribute created directly in the class body can be shared across instances, which is often an unwanted surprise for beginners.

A method call such as session.finish() passes the instance to its method automatically. Keep the method’s state change understandable and protect domain constraints where needed. Public attributes are not automatically validated simply because they belong to a class. The examples focus on separate instance state and a clear method contract; inheritance is not required to organise this small model.

## Example 1: Create an instance

```python
class Session:
    def __init__(self, subject, minutes):
        self.subject = subject
        self.minutes = minutes

session = Session("Python", 30)
print(session.subject)
print(session.minutes)
```

Expected output:

```text
Python
30
```

The constructor arguments initialise two attributes on the new instance. The class defines the structure; the session name refers to one concrete instance.

## Example 2: Keep per-instance state separate

```python
class Checklist:
    def __init__(self):
        self.items = []

first = Checklist()
second = Checklist()
first.items.append("Read")
print(first.items)
print(second.items)
```

Expected output:

```text
['Read']
[]
```

A fresh list is created in each initialisation. Appending to the first instance’s items does not append to the second instance’s separate list.

## Example 3: Call a state-changing method

```python
class Session:
    def __init__(self):
        self.completed = False

    def finish(self):
        self.completed = True

session = Session()
print(session.completed)
session.finish()
print(session.completed)
```

Expected output:

```text
False
True
```

finish receives the instance and changes its completed attribute. The call, not the mere method definition, performs the change.

## Check the reasoning

Instance attributes assigned through self belong to that instance rather than an implicitly shared mutable class collection.

A matching screenshot or output is one check, not proof that a program is correct for all inputs. Change one input, predict the new result and run again. If the result differs, find the first instruction where your prediction stops matching the program state. Keep that small case as a regression check when you fix the cause.

## Understand the idea

A test compares observed behaviour with an explicit expectation. It is stronger than glancing at output and deciding it looks plausible. Start with a small function whose return contract is clear, then cover a normal case, a boundary and a failure case. A passing example proves that particular check, not every possible property of the program.

Assertions are convenient for small learning checks, but ordinary assert statements can be disabled when Python runs with optimisation. Do not use assert as the only protection for user input, authentication or another required production invariant. Explicit validation should raise or return an intentional failure independently of optimisation settings. unittest supplies test-case methods for a structured suite.

Debugging begins with reproducing the defect. Reduce the input, locate the first point where observed state differs from the prediction, and fix the cause rather than editing the expected output until the test turns green. Keep a regression check that would have failed before the fix. A test that never calls the relevant function, or only repeats its implementation in a different spelling, can create false confidence.

## Example 1: Check an exact return value

```python
def total(days, minutes):
    return days * minutes

assert total(5, 30) == 150
assert total(0, 30) == 0
print("Two checks passed")
```

Expected output:

```text
Two checks passed
```

The second assertion tests the zero-day boundary. The message is printed only after both assertions succeed in this normal interpreter configuration.

## Example 2: Check a required failure

```python
def checked_minutes(value):
    if value < 0:
        raise ValueError("Negative duration")
    return value

try:
    checked_minutes(-1)
except ValueError:
    print("Expected rejection")
else:
    raise RuntimeError("Missing rejection")
```

Expected output:

```text
Expected rejection
```

The else branch would fail the check if the invalid input were accepted. Merely catching an exception without an explicit no-exception failure would not prove the rejection happened.

## Example 3: Use a structured test case

```python
import unittest

class TotalChecks(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_product(self):
        self.assertEqual(5 * 30, 150)

result = unittest.TestResult()
TotalChecks("test_product").run(result)
print(result.testsRun)
print(result.wasSuccessful())
```

Expected output:

```text
1
True
```

The test case executes one named test and records its result without printing an environment-dependent runner banner. A real application would test its actual function rather than only this introductory arithmetic expression.

## Check the reasoning

Test normal cases, boundaries and expected failures; a passing test does not prove all possible behaviour.

A matching screenshot or output is one check, not proof that a program is correct for all inputs. Change one input, predict the new result and run again. If the result differs, find the first instruction where your prediction stops matching the program state. Keep that small case as a regression check when you fix the cause.

## Understand the idea

This project combines the core tools into a small revision planner without introducing a paid service or a web framework. Its input is a bounded list of session records; its output is a readable summary of planned and completed minutes. Keep collection processing separate from display so that calculations can be tested independently.

Each record needs a subject, nonnegative integer minutes and a completed boolean. Define those requirements before writing the loop. Reject bad records explicitly instead of silently converting them into zero-minute sessions. A bool is a subclass of int in Python, so type(value) is int is a useful exact-type check when True must not count as one minute. This detail illustrates why validation rules should express the domain precisely.

Start with hard-coded sample data and pure functions. Add JSON import/export only after the calculations and validation pass checks. In browser practice, this means parsing and printing JSON text, not promising durable file storage. A graphical interface, database and network synchronisation are separate future projects. A clear, well-tested console tool is a complete result for this scope.

Work in small checkpoints: validate one record, total two records, calculate completed minutes, then format the report. Verify empty input, all incomplete sessions, all complete sessions and one invalid duration. Keep the first project small enough that you can explain every line without relying on unexplained libraries.

## Example 1: Total the planned minutes

```python
sessions = [
    {"subject": "Python", "minutes": 30, "done": True},
    {"subject": "HTML", "minutes": 20, "done": False},
]
planned = sum(session["minutes"] for session in sessions)
print(planned)
```

Expected output:

```text
50
```

The generator expression supplies each duration to sum. The result is planned time, not completed time: completion status has not been used as a filter.

## Example 2: Count completed minutes

```python
sessions = [
    {"minutes": 30, "done": True},
    {"minutes": 20, "done": False},
]
completed = sum(session["minutes"] for session in sessions if session["done"])
print(completed)
```

Expected output:

```text
30
```

The condition includes only completed sessions. This is a minutes total, not merely the number of completed records. Keep those measures separate in the final report.

## Example 3: Validate and report through a function

```python
def report(sessions):
    for session in sessions:
```
